title: DELUGE: Big Projects First, High-Margin After-Sales For Years
article:
Deluge Corporation may not be a household name, but its project references certainly are: Marina Bay Sands, the North-South Corridor, MRT lines and data centres in Johor.

Listed on 16 Oct at
60 cents
, the Singapore company, which closed at 62 cents on 22 Oct, designs, installs and maintains fire-detection and protection systems.
Think sprinklers, alarms and specialised systems that suppress fires in sensitive environments.

Deluge executive chairman Vincent Cheo (right) with CEO Lee Wai Wah.

8.3% market share
in 2025, according to Frost & Sullivan research cited in its IPO materials.

Big projects, substantial backlog

Deluge is one of eight contractors holding the highest BCA grading for fire-protection work, allowing it to tender for public-sector projects without a value ceiling.

Arguably, that experience and technical requirements further narrow the field for complex jobs.
Its advantages include established supplier relationships and prefabrication.

That represents substantial secured work, which is expected to be mainly fulfilled over the next four financial years.

Management says the decline needs some context: FY2025 was unusually strong as several major projects reached peak execution, while FY2026 represented a normalisation in activity.

The more profitable second act

Deluge’s Lifecycle Services business handles maintenance, repairs, upgrades and alterations to existing systems.

In FY2026, it contributed approximately

More strikingly, its
53.1% gross margin
was over twice Integrated Projects’ 24.8%, allowing services to generate roughly half the group’s gross profit.

title: CPF, SSB, T-Bills or Dividend Stocks: Where Should Retirees Put Their Money?
article:
All is not lost even if you only start to invest in your 50s as a retiree.
However, at this stage, investing is less about growing wealth and more about ensuring a dependable income that can support you throughout retirement.
Singapore retirees have several options, including the Central Provident Fund (CPF), Singapore Savings Bonds (SSBs), Treasury bills (T-bills) and dividend-paying stocks.
CPF: A Foundation for Retirement Income
CPF is one of the simplest ways to grow retirement savings, risk-free, with capital guaranteed, even if returns are conservative.
The CPF Ordinary Account (OA) currently earns 2.5% per annum.
The Special, MediSave and Retirement accounts earn 4.0% per annum, a floor the Government has extended to 31 December 2027.
Members aged 55 and above earn an extra 2% on the first S$30,000 of combined balances and an extra 1% on the next S$30,000.
Retirees can take advantage of the safe interest by topping up their accounts with cash, but they should understand that CPF savings are subject to withdrawal rules and restrictions.
Through CPF Lifelong Income For the Elderly (CPF LIFE), a national longevity annuity scheme, eligible Singaporeans also receive monthly payouts no matter how long they live.
However, payouts are dependent on factors such as the payout plan and commencement age.
Related articles:
Secret Formula to Balance CPF Savings and Stock Investing for the Long Term
How to Outperform the 4% CPF SA Rate with S$30,000
Singapore Savings Bonds: Flexibility with Capital Protection
Backed by the Singapore Government, Singapore Savings Bonds (SSBs) are capital-guaranteed with a maximum tenure of 10 years.
You can choose to exit your investment in any given month with no penalties.
Compared to CPF, SSBs come with greater flexibility, as the minimum redemption amount is merely S$500.
The maximum amount of SSBs that each investor may hold at any one time is S$200,000.
A non-refundable transaction fee of S$2 applies to each application and redemption request, regardless of whether the application is successful or not.
Sounds good?
The catch is that SSBs’ interest rates vary and can potentially be lower than CPF’s.
The November 2026 SSB pays 1.67% in its first year, rising to 3.08% in year 10.
That works out to an average of 2.45% a year if held for the full 10 years.
Early redemption means investors do not receive the full advertised 10-year average return.
T-Bills: Short-Term Returns with Government Backing
T-bills are 6-month and 1-year Singapore Government Securities issued at a discount to their face value, and investors receive the full face value at maturity.
Being government-backed and short-dated, T-bills are useful for managing near-term cash needs.
Returns are known when the bill is successfully allotted and held to maturity.
While the investment period is short, money is typically committed until maturity.
Selling a T-bill before maturity on the secondary market could mean a loss.
For retirees who might not need the money immediately, there is also reinvestment risk as maturing T-bills might be replaced at potentially lower yields.
Related articles:
T-Bills vs. Dividend Stocks: Why a 25-Year-Old Should Be Taking More Risk in 2026
REIT Yields vs T-Bills: Has the Gap Widened Again?
Dividend Stocks: Higher Income Potential, but Greater Risk
With dividend stocks, retirees are investing for recurring income and potential capital appreciation, albeit with higher risks.
Quality Singapore dividend stocks such as
DBS Group
(SGX: D05),
Singtel
(SGX: Z74) and
Singapore Exchange
(SGX: S68) currently offer dividend yields of between 2.2% to 4.5% on a trailing basis.
DBS has seen 148.6% share price growth over the past three years, from S$30.01 per share on 23 October 2023 to S$74.59 on 22 October 2026.
Its dividend has grown alongside its profits, which have historically supported its payouts.
Growing dividends can also help retirees keep pace with inflation.
Back in 2001, DBS paid dividends twice a year, totalling S$0.23 per share after adjusting for later rights and bonus issues.
Today, its ordinary dividend alone is nearly three times that amount every quarter.
It also paid S$0.60 in capital return dividends in FY2025, which it plans to continue only through FY2027
While dividend stocks come with the potential for higher income, share prices can fall significantly, wiping out capital in worst-case scenarios.
Dividends are also not guaranteed and may be reduced.
Instead of chasing
high yields
, investors should pay attention to cash flow and balance sheet strength, making sure the dividends are backed by sustainable earnings and not debt.
Related articles:
CPF vs Dividend Stocks: Which Could Generate More Income Over 10 Years?
CPF, Fixed Deposits or Dividend Stocks: Where Should You Put S$50,000?
How Do They Compare?
If you are just looking at returns,
CPF:
Up to 5% per annum on the first S$60,000 in combined savings
SSBs:
Average return over 10 years at 2.45% for the November issue
6-month T-bills:
1.90% cut-off yield for the 13 October 2026 issue
1-year T-bills:
1.92% cut-off yield for the 20 October 2026 issue
Dividend stocks:
DBS at 4.3% yield, and Singtel at 4.4%
However, yields shouldn’t be the only factor you look at.
Comparing CPF, SSBs, T-bills and dividend stocks comes down to understanding and balancing a few core factors:

Retirees should not simply look at the highest yields, but rather at their income needs and risk tolerance.
How I Would Allocate Retirement Savings
Different retirees have different needs during their golden years.
if I were a retiree with S$300,000, this would be how I
allocate my money
:
30% in SSBs: Liquidity and to minimise reinvestment risk
20% in T-bills: Ensure liquidity with interest
40% in diversified dividend stocks: Offer the potential for higher income
10% in cash: For any unexpected spending needs
CPF LIFE functions as part of a retiree’s existing income foundation, covering everyday expenses rather than serving as freely investable capital.
Adjust the allocation according to your financial obligations and spending needs.
An older retiree with lower risk tolerance can increase their T-bill allocation while reducing their dividend stock allocation, and a younger retiree can have more in dividend stocks and SSBs.
Get Smart: Don’t Put All Your Retirement Eggs in One Basket
Investing as a retiree is not an either-or situation.
CPF LIFE provides a foundation of lifelong income, while SSBs and T-bills help preserve capital and manage shorter-term financial needs.
Dividend stocks offer the potential for higher income and long-term growth but come with higher risks.
Retirees can consider combining them to balance safety, income, liquidity and growth, giving both peace of mind and support for their
retirement
needs.

title: Asian stocks to slide on tech rout, bonds rally
article:
(Oct 23) : Asian stocks were set to extend losses Friday, tracking a slump on Wall Street as a rout in technology giants and escalating Middle East hostilities drove investors toward the safety of bonds.

Equity-index futures for Japan, Australia and South Korea all fell, pointing to a second straight decline for a regional stock gauge after it dropped Thursday to the lowest since late July.

US stock futures steadied in early trading after the Nasdaq 100 tumbled 2.9% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank 6.7%, their biggest declines since late June. The S&P 500 fell 1.2%, with Meta Platforms Inc. among the megacaps hit after investors parsed its results.

The risk-off move spread across markets. Treasuries staged their biggest rally in more than a year, sending the 10-year yield down about 17 basis points to 4.95%, while the yen outperformed all its major counterparts. Brent crude topped US$113 a barrel as deadly attacks in Saudi Arabia heightened concerns over supplies. Australian sovereign debt tracked the moves in Treasuries in early Asian trading.

Technology megacaps that have powered a four-year bull run in US equities bore the brunt of the selling. Mixed results from companies including Meta and Tesla Inc. added to concerns that the group’s rebound since late March had gone too far, too quickly.

“Sentiment seems to be shakier these days as investors reconsider AI-related assets,” said Eugene Leow, senior rates strategist at DBS Bank Ltd. “With US yields still elevated by recent standards, investors may want to hedge off some of these risks by seeking safety in Treasuries.”

See also: US proposes curbs on investment in Chinese biotech firms

Treasuries surged across the curve Thursday as the deepening rout in AI-related shares, turmoil in French markets and renewed Middle East tensions fueled haven buying. The rally pushed the 10-year yield below 5% for the first time in a month, with buying in Treasury futures accelerating as traders unwound bearish positions.

Concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence investment and its eventual payoff have knocked technology shares from recent highs and are beginning to weigh on the broader economic outlook. Traders also pared expectations for another Federal Reserve interest-rate increase this year.

Elsewhere, oil extended gains. A drone strike on Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah field killed two people without disrupting operations, while an attack on King Fahd International Airport caused casualties. Houthi rebels also claimed strikes on the Saudi port of Yanbu.

See also: Stocks fall as AI jitters ease bets on Fed hikes

“It feels like just a risk-off day and tech is always the first to get hit,” said Joseph Saluzzi, partner and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading LLC. “The bond rally also confirms the risk-off approach.” Investors are concerned that “post-election, the Iran war may escalate and potentially continue for a longer time than anticipated,” he added.

In Asia, Chinese stocks will be in focus after a US$2.4 trillion slide from their May peak pushed them into a bear market. Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. suffered its steepest drop in two months Thursday, helping drag the Hang Seng Tech Index down 5%, its biggest decline since April 2025, as weak consumption and concerns over AI profitability weighed on the market.

“Investor sentiment remains very poor for China’s onshore and offshore markets, and without new policy or tech catalysts, this kind of volatile, directionless environment may persist into early 2027,” said Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier in Singapore.

title: US proposes curbs on investment in Chinese biotech firms
article:
(Oct 23) : The Trump administration is seeking to restrict American investment in Chinese biotechnology companies, potentially complicating financial ties at a time when US drugmakers are increasingly turning to China for new medicines.

The US Treasury Department on Thursday proposed adding biotechnology to a list of sensitive technologies subject to restrictions on American investment in foreign adversaries, citing national security concerns.

The proposed regulations would require American investors to notify the government about certain transactions involving foreign companies developing sensitive technologies and prohibit others entirely. The rules would expand an existing program targeting investments in areas including artificial intelligence, semiconductors and quantum computing.

Chinese biotechnology companies have become a source of innovation for the pharmaceutical industry. US drugmakers are increasingly turning to China to license promising treatments as they search for new products to replenish their pipelines.

The proposed regulations would also restrict investment in Chinese brain-computer interface companies, a growing field of startups that aim to build technologies that allow people to control electronics directly with their brains. China and the US both have burgeoning brain tech industries, with startups racing to develop implants, helmets and other devices.

The restrictions could complicate investments in Chinese biotechnology companies, though their impact on pharmaceutical partnerships remains unclear. The Treasury Department is seeking public comments before issuing a final rule. The restrictions won’t take effect until that process is complete.

See also: Stocks fall as AI jitters ease bets on Fed hikes

title: Stocks fall as AI jitters ease bets on Fed hikes
article:
(Oct 23) : Wall Street shunned stocks as a technology rout and Middle East risks drove investors to the safety of bonds, reducing bets on another Federal Reserve rate hike in 2026.

A nearly 7% plunge in chipmakers sent the Nasdaq 100 to its worst day since June. That was after Meta Platforms Inc.’s plans to boost capital spending reignited fears that tech firms will issue more debt to finance the artificial-intelligence buildout. The S&P 500 fell 1.2%. An oil rally also weighed on sentiment amid heightened supply fears.

The rush for shelter spurred the biggest jump in Treasuries in over a year, outweighing worries about energy-fueled inflation. In fact, money markets are no longer fully pricing in a Fed rate increase by the end of the year.

“The correction in tech valuations prompted investors to reconsider whether a market-induced tightening of financial conditions could warrant a less restrictive course of monetary policy,” said Ian Lyngen at BMO Capital Markets.

Following an extraordinary run in tech stocks, markets are becoming more demanding around evidence of the payoff from AI investments and worries about the sustainability of that spending amid higher rates, according to James McCann at Edward Jones.

“We remain constructive on large-cap stocks,” he said. “However, investors should look to ensure that they have good diversification in portfolios.”

See also: Oil rises as deadly Saudi attack fans Middle East supply fears

Meta’s results kicked off a technology earnings season that’s likely to focus on runaway AI expenditures — and attempts by companies to get a return on investment. Alphabet Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Amazon.com Inc., three of the other biggest spenders on data centers, are slated to report next week.

Blackstone Inc. President Jon Gray said investors don’t need to worry that the boom in AI will turn into a bubble, just days after billionaire Ken Griffin said he fears the industry was “almost certainly” headed in that direction.

“When you think about a bubble, you think about building capacity and then hoping the demand comes,” Gray told Bloomberg Television after the firm reported its third-quarter results. “With AI, you’re building capacity, and you’re hoping you can keep up with the demand.”

See also: Stocks climb in late hours on Meta’s big AI wagers

Elsewhere, Chinese stocks were dragged into a bear market, with US$2.4 trillion lost since a peak in May, as a protracted slump in consumption and mounting doubts over the profitability of AI companies turn them into one of the world’s worst performers.

Meantime, French bond stress deepened as spreads widened to a 15-year high, with a broad flight from risk and the threat of another weekend of protests reinforcing the country’s status as the weak link in global markets.
